title: Asana Center: Help Center, Academy and Forum Guide
summary: Looking for the Asana Center? Here is where the Help Center, Academy and Forum live, what each one does, and how security and GRC teams can use them.
body_markdown:
When people search for the "Asana center," they almost always want one of three things: the Asana Help Center for step-by-step documentation, Asana Academy for structured training, or the Asana Community Forum for peer answers. Asana describes all three on a single page,[How to use Asana help resources](https://help.asana.com/s/article/how-to-use-asana-help-resources) , and we walk through each one below, along with a few practical notes for security, risk and compliance teams who run questionnaire work inside Asana.

[Explore questionnaire automation](https://skypher.co/)


## TL;DR


- The **Help Center** is the reference library: documentation, troubleshooting, integrations and admin controls.
- **Asana Academy** is the learning path: self-paced courses and live sessions for beginners, admins and team leads.
- The **Community Forum** is where you ask other users questions and share how you work.
- Asana, Inc. is headquartered at 633 Folsom Street, Suite 100, San Francisco, CA 94107, according to its[annual report filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477720/000147772026000021/asan-20260131.htm) .
- For security questionnaires, a work management tool tracks tasks well, but the answering itself is better handled by a purpose-built platform.

## What people mean by "Asana center"


Asana does not have one product called the Asana Center. The phrase is shorthand, and the search results reflect that: the top pages are the Help Center home, Asana Academy, the Getting Started section and the video tutorials. A few unrelated results appear too, such as a local class schedule and an Atlassian Marketplace listing for a Jira Data Center integration, which only share the words in the query.


If you landed here from a search, use this quick map:


You want to... Go to Best for


Look up how a feature works Help Center Admins, project owners, anyone stuck on a setting


Learn the platform in a structured way Asana Academy New users, team leads, implementers


Ask a question or see how others work Community Forum Practical, real-world questions


Watch a short walkthrough Video tutorials in the Help Center Visual learners


The rest of this guide goes through each in turn, then shifts to what matters if your team is in security, GRC or sales engineering.


## The Asana Help Center


The[Asana Help Center](https://help.asana.com/s/) is the first stop for anything operational. Its home page opens with a "New to Asana?" entry point for beginners and a support option, and it also has a dedicated route for Asana Gov customers. Beneath that sits the documentation for individual features.


According to Asana's own[help resources page](https://help.asana.com/s/article/how-to-use-asana-help-resources) , the Help Center is where you find step-by-step documentation, including troubleshooting. Several features carry a "Who can use this feature?" label that lists the plans it applies to, such as Personal, Starter, Advanced, Enterprise and Enterprise+. We suggest checking that label first, because a feature that is documented is not necessarily available on your plan.


### Where to start inside the Help Center


1. **Getting started.** The guide for[new users who have been invited to Asana](https://help.asana.com/s/article/you-ve-been-invited-to-asana-now-what?language=en_US) explains that Asana works on web and mobile, then walks through the first steps.
2. **All features.** The[full feature index](https://help.asana.com/s/article/all-asana-features?language=en_US) is the fastest way to see what the platform covers, from workspace setup to integrations and automation permissions.
3. **Video tutorials.** Short clips cover the basics and are useful when you need to show a colleague quickly.


### A tip for admins


If you manage Asana for a department, read the Admin Console documentation early. Controls you set at the start, such as who can create projects and how teams are organized, are far easier than cleaning up after the fact. Teams that skip this tend to end up with project sprawl, meaning dozens of near-duplicate projects with inconsistent naming, and that is tedious to remediate later.


## Asana Academy


Where the Help Center answers "how do I do this," Asana Academy answers "how should we work." Asana's resources page describes it as the place for structured learning, with self-paced courses and live training. In practice that means fundamentals for beginners, courses on building workflows, and training aimed at specific roles. There is also a separate learning area for nonprofit and education organizations, which shows up in the search results.


If you want a detailed walkthrough of the courses and certification options, we cover them in our guide to[Asana Academy courses and certification](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/asana-academy) .


### Who should invest the time


- **New team members** who were invited into an existing workspace and need the basics in an hour or two.
- **Team leads** who are responsible for how a team uses projects, portfolios and goals.
- **Admins and implementers** who are rolling out Asana to a department and want a repeatable standard.


One habit we have seen pay off: before anyone builds a project, agree on naming conventions and templates. Academy material on workflow building is most valuable when it feeds a written standard that the whole team follows.


## The Community Forum


The third resource is the Asana Community Forum. Asana's[Forum basics article](https://help.asana.com/s/article/asana-community-forum-basics?language=en_US) covers how to join, connect the Forum with your Asana account, complete your profile, post a topic and manage notifications. It is the right place for questions that documentation does not answer directly, such as how another company structured a review process or how people handle a niche integration.


Treat forum answers as peer advice. For anything involving permissions, data handling or compliance, confirm against the official documentation or Asana support before you change a setting.


## Where is Asana headquartered, and is it still a going concern?


Two of the questions Google surfaces for this topic are about the company itself, and they matter if you are doing vendor due diligence.


**Headquarters.** Asana's[SEC filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477720/000147772026000021/asan-20260131.htm) lists its principal executive offices at 633 Folsom Street, Suite 100, San Francisco, CA 94107. A[GlobalData profile](https://www.globaldata.com/company-profile/asana-inc/locations/) gives the same address.


**Is Asana still used?** Yes. In the same filing, the company reports more than 180,000 paying customers as of January 31, 2026, and fiscal 2026 revenue of $790.8 million, up 9% on the prior year. Those numbers come from the company's own report, so read them as the vendor's statement, not an independent ranking.


**Direction of the product.** Asana now calls itself the system of action for work, built for what it terms the Agentic Enterprise, where people and AI agents collaborate in a shared, governed setup. For a CISO or GRC lead, the point to take away is practical: as AI takes on more tasks, you will want an audit trail that covers both human and automated actions, and you should ask any vendor how it provides one.


## Using Asana for security and compliance work


Many of our readers are CISOs, GRC managers, solution engineers and sales directors, and plenty of them already run Asana. It is a sensible tool for coordinating security questionnaire work, as long as you use it for what it does well.


### What Asana does well here


- **Assigning and tracking.** Each incoming questionnaire becomes a project or a task with owners, due dates and subtasks per section.
- **Connecting work to goals.** Portfolios and goals let you link security maturity targets to the individual tasks behind them, so leadership sees progress without asking for a status update.
- **Admin oversight.** The Admin Console and its API-driven controls help you govern who can see and change workflows, which supports your own audit conversations.


### A simple setup for questionnaire intake


1. Create a project template with sections for intake, assignment, subject-matter review, approval and delivery.
2. Add a custom field for the customer, the framework (for example SIG, CAIQ or a custom format) and the deadline.
3. Use a form or request intake so that sales can submit new questionnaires without messaging you directly.
4. Assign each section to its owner: security, legal, IT, or product.
5. Review closed projects monthly and update the template.


This gives you visibility. It does not write the answers.


### Where task managers stop


The slow part of a security questionnaire is rarely the tracking. It is finding the right answer in policies, past responses and documents, adapting it to the question's wording, and keeping it consistent across dozens of customers. A task manager holds the work item, not the knowledge behind it. Teams that rely on spreadsheets and copy-paste inside a project tend to find that the same questions get answered by hand again and again.


## Our perspective


We build Skypher, so we see this from the questionnaire side. Our view is that work management and questionnaire automation solve different problems, and the strongest setups use both.


A work management tool answers "who is doing what by when." A questionnaire platform answers "what is the right, approved answer to this question, and how confident are we?" We designed Skypher around the second question. It parses every format your customers send, retrieves answers from your own knowledge base using proprietary retrieval AI, and shows a confidence score so reviewers know where to spend their attention. It connects to the places your content already lives, including Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, OneDrive and SharePoint, and to Slack and Microsoft Teams, so subject-matter experts can respond where they already work.


If you coordinate in Asana, you do not have to abandon that. Keep Asana as the system for ownership and deadlines, and let automation handle the first draft of the answers. The people in your team then spend their time on review and on the unusual questions, which is where their expertise matters.


We would also encourage you to define your conventions first, whichever tools you pick. A clean template, clear owners and a maintained knowledge base make any platform work better, ours included.

## A practical checklist for getting more from the Asana Center


- Bookmark the Help Center and the feature index, and check the plan label before planning around a feature.
- Send new admins to Academy before they build anything.
- Write down naming conventions, templates and permission rules in one page.
- Use the Forum for ideas, and the official documentation for decisions.
- Review your workflows each quarter, and ask whether any step is repetitive enough to automate.


## FAQ


### Where is the Asana Help Center?


It lives at help.asana.com, and it is linked from within the Asana product as well. The home page offers beginner resources, support options and documentation by feature. Asana also publishes an article that explains how the Help Center, Academy and Forum fit together.


### What is the difference between the Help Center and Asana Academy?


The Help Center is documentation: you look something up, follow the steps and go back to work. Academy is training: courses and live sessions that teach you how to work well in the platform. Most teams use the Help Center daily and Academy at onboarding or rollout.


### Where is Asana headquartered in the US?


Asana's principal executive offices are at 633 Folsom Street, Suite 100, San Francisco, CA 94107, as stated in its annual report filed with the SEC for the fiscal year ended January 31, 2026. Addresses can change, so check the company's latest filing if you need it for a contract.


### Is Asana still being used?


Yes. The company reported more than 180,000 paying customers as of January 31, 2026. It is a publicly traded company, so its filings are the best place to check current figures.


### Can Asana handle security questionnaires on its own?


It can track them well, with owners, deadlines and approvals. Drafting accurate answers from your policies and past responses is a different job, which is where a dedicated questionnaire platform helps.
